blocks.en: Abstract
blocks.zh: 摘要

blocks.en: Large language models often produce hallucinated answers, motivating selective prediction policies that abstain on uncertain queries. However, heuristic uncertainty thresholds alone do not provide statistical control of errors among accepted predictions. Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) reduce selection-conditioned error rate (SCER) calibration to a nonpositive expected linear-loss constraint, but the associated loss is non-monotonic in the acceptance threshold. We construct an exact counterexample under i.i.d. sampling demonstrating that LEC's empirical threshold-selection rule can violate the population SCER target. To address this risk-transfer gap, we introduce Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control (SC-LEC), which uses the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference to compensate for threshold-selection instability. For local expansion beyond a safe anchor, we derive two finite-sample certificates: a stability-based certificate exploiting rank crossings and a direct certificate using the structure of threshold expansion to reduce conservatism. With a valid population anchor margin, our certificate conditions ensure finite-sample marginal SCER control, and independent margin certification further provides a $1-δ$ high-probability guarantee for this calibration-averaged control. Experiments on CommonsenseQA, ARC-Challenge, and TriviaQA show useful retention gains beyond the same certified anchor, while revealing conservative behavior in small-margin regimes.

blocks.en: 1 Introduction
blocks.zh: 导言

blocks.en:
Large language models (LLMs) have demonstrated strong capabilities in question answering, yet remain susceptible to hallucinations and overconfident errors ( Huang et al., 2025 ) .
Selective prediction offers a practical way to improve reliability by abstaining on uncertain queries rather than answering indiscriminately ( El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010 ; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019 ) .
Uncertainty measures such as semantic entropy help determine which predictions to accept ( Kuhn et al., 2023 ; Duan et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025a ) .
However, a reliable uncertainty ranking does not, by itself, guarantee that the error rate among accepted predictions is statistically controlled.

选择性预测通过放弃不确定的询问而不是不加区分地回答,提供了一个提高可靠性的实际方法(El-Yaniv和Wiener,2010年;Geifman和El-Yaniv,2019年)。

然而,可靠的不确定性排名本身并不能保证接受的预测中的错误率在统计学上得到控制。

Our objective is to control the marginal selection-conditioned error rate (SCER), defined as the ratio of expected accepted errors to expected selections, on average over both calibration and future observations ( El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010 ; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017 ) .
Linear Expectation Constraints (LEC) ( Wang et al., 2026a ) reduce this ratio-form objective to a linear expectation constraint, 𝔼 ⁡ [ ( E − α ) ​ S ] ≤ 0 \mathbb{E}[(E-\alpha)S]\leq 0 , where E E and S S denote prediction error and selection, respectively, and α \alpha is the risk level.
Yet, this linearization alone does not resolve the challenge of adaptive threshold calibration ( Angelopoulos, 2026 ) .
The induced loss is non-monotonic: accepting a correct prediction decreases the cumulative linear loss by α \alpha , whereas accepting an incorrect prediction increases it by 1 − α 1-\alpha .
Consequently, standard monotonic calibration arguments do not directly justify selecting the largest empirically feasible threshold.
An exact i.i.d. counterexample shows that the original LEC complete-scan rule can violate the population SCER target (Figure 4 ).
Moreover, a positive expected linear-risk slack β \beta yields only SCER ≤ α + β / r \mathrm{SCER}\leq\alpha+\beta/r , where r r denotes marginal retention, making exact control particularly challenging when retention is small.

blocks.en:
We propose Stability-Compensated Linear Expectation Control ( SC-LEC ), which establishes finite-sample guarantees for anchored non-monotonic threshold calibration.
As shown in Figure 1 , SC-LEC compensates for threshold-selection instability using the negative linear risk of a theoretical full-data reference.
Building on the stability-transfer perspective of Angelopoulos (2026) , we decompose the deployed linear risk into a safety reserve and a signed stability gap.
When the reserve dominates a valid upper bound on this gap, the resulting linear risk remains nonpositive, recovering the desired marginal SCER control.
To make this principle operational, we introduce an anchored local-search procedure and derive two complementary finite-sample certificates: a stability-based certificate that exploits directional rank crossings and a direct certificate that uses the structure of one-dimensional threshold expansion to reduce conservatism.
Independent margin certification further enables the certificates to be constructed from samples without requiring a known population margin.

blocks.en:
These results address both the risk-transfer gap and its practical certification:
Firstly, we identify a failure of empirical non-monotonic threshold calibration through an exact population counterexample and specialize reserve–stability analysis to the selection-conditioned linear-risk target.
Moreover, we develop structure-aware finite-sample certificates for anchored threshold search, including directional and local-crossing stability bounds and a tighter direct analysis that reduces certification conservatism.
An executable calibration procedure combines independent margin certification with automatic buffer and window selection.
With valid population margins, the resulting designs achieve finite-sample marginal SCER control, while independently certified margins provide a 1 − δ 1-\delta high-probability guarantee of this calibration-averaged control.
Experiments across three QA benchmarks show expansion beyond a common safe anchor and limited certification in small-margin regimes.

此外,我们为锚定阈值搜索开发结构意识有限样本证书,包括方向和局部交叉稳定性界限以及更严格的直接分析,以减少认证保守主义。
一个可执行的校准程序结合了独立比值认证与自动缓冲和窗口选择.
有了有效的人口边距,由此产生的设计就实现了有限-抽样的边际SCER控制,而独立认证的边距则为这种校准-平均控制提供了1− 1- delta高概率保障。

blocks.en: 2 Related Work
blocks.zh: 2 相关工作

blocks.en:
Selective Prediction and Risk Calibration. Selective prediction improves reliability by allowing models to abstain on uncertain inputs, trading prediction coverage for reduced error ( El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010 ; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017 ; Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019 ) .
For language generation, semantic uncertainty estimates uncertainty by clustering equivalent outputs ( Kuhn et al., 2023 ; Farquhar et al., 2024 ; Lin et al., 2024 ) . Conformal approaches also study uncertainty and selection in language models ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) .
Yet, uncertainty quantification does not ensure statistical reliability, motivating calibration methods with explicit risk guarantees.
Conformal prediction offers distribution-free coverage guarantees ( Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023 ; Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) , while conformal risk control (CRC) extends this perspective to monotonic expected losses ( Angelopoulos et al., 2024 ) .
Learn then Test further enables high-probability risk control through statistical testing ( Bates et al., 2021 ; Angelopoulos et al., 2025 ) .
COIN studies calibrated abstention for question answering ( Wang et al., 2026b ) , while Trust or Escalate studies selective LLM judging with human-agreement guarantees ( Jung et al., 2025 ) .
These studies motivate statistically rigorous selection, but differ in their risk targets and calibration procedures.

blocks.en:
Linear and Non-Monotonic Calibration. LEC frames marginal selection-conditioned error control as a linear expectation constraint ( Wang et al., 2026a ) , providing a foundation for selective prediction and routing ( Jia et al., 2026 ) .
Although this reduction is exact, the resulting loss is non-monotonic in the acceptance threshold, and empirical feasibility alone does not justify population risk control under adaptive selection.
We demonstrate this limitation via an exact counterexample to LEC’s unrestricted complete-scan rule in Appendix B.10 .
Related approaches address non-monotonicity through different mechanisms: monotonized calibration provides asymptotic control ( Lin and Dong, 2026 ) , whereas finite-grid analyses establish sample-dependent risk bounds ( Aldirawi et al., 2026 ) .
SC-LEC studies calibration-generated thresholds through anchored local search with explicit risk compensation for finite-sample marginal SCER control.
Further connections are discussed in Appendix D .

Stability of Threshold Calibration. Our work is closely related to the framework of Angelopoulos (2026) , which transfers expected loss from a full-data reference to a calibration-fitted rule for non-monotonic risk control.
This analysis also develops rank-crossing bounds for selective classification, which our analysis builds on.
Nonetheless, for the shifted selective loss ℓ ~ α = g α + α \widetilde{\ell}_{\alpha}=g_{\alpha}+\alpha , an expected-loss bound with additive slack β \beta yields SCER ≤ α + β r \operatorname{SCER}\leq\alpha+\frac{\beta}{r} , where r = 𝔼 ⁡ [ S ] > 0 r=\mathbb{E}[S]>0 , from the linear-risk identity alone, making the slack sensitive to marginal retention.
SC-LEC instead targets the nonpositive linear-risk endpoint by explicitly compensating threshold-selection instability with a sufficient safety reserve.

blocks.en: 5 Conclusion
blocks.zh: 5 结论

blocks.en:
In this paper, we identify an exact i.i.d. counterexample that establishes a gap between empirical feasibility and marginal SCER control in LEC’s adaptive threshold search.
Building on stability-based risk transfer, SC-LEC compensates for threshold-selection instability using the negative risk of a full-data reference.
Furthermore, SC-S develops bounds on this instability through local rank crossings, while SC-D directly bounds the risk of anchored expansion and permits wider windows under the specified shared-design conditions.
With valid population margins, both certificates ensure finite-sample marginal SCER control at positive retention.
Independent margin certification provides an upstream 1 − δ 1-\delta certificate of this calibration-averaged guarantee.
Empirical evaluations on three QA datasets demonstrate retention gains beyond the same safe anchor and show how anchor selection and small certified margins affect those gains.
blocks.zh:
在本文中,我们确定了一个确切的“d”实例,在LEC适应性阈值搜索中确定经验可行性与边际SCER控制之间的差距。
在稳定风险转移的基础上,SC-LEC利用全数据参考的负面风险来补偿阈值选择不稳定。
此外,SC-S通过地方等级过境点对这种不稳定情况形成界限,而SC-D直接限制锚定扩展的风险,允许在规定的共享设计条件下扩大窗口。
有了有效的人口边距,两个证书都保证在正留存时进行有限-抽样的边际SCER控制。

blocks.en:
Selective prediction trades coverage for accuracy by allowing a model to
abstain ( El-Yaniv and Wiener, 2010 ) . In QA, the usefulness of abstention
depends on whether confidence identifies questions the model is likely to
answer correctly. Kamath et al. (2020) study selective QA under
domain shift and train an error-predicting calibrator using in-domain and
out-of-domain examples. Their setting motivates studying abstention beyond
raw model probabilities, although our guarantees assume the stated
exchangeability or i.i.d. conditions. Training can also change a model’s
refusal behavior: R-Tuning constructs refusal-aware instruction data so
that LLMs learn when to answer and when to decline ( Zhang et al., 2024 ) .
Similarly, SelectiveNet jointly learns prediction and
rejection ( Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2019 ) , whereas SGR calibrates a selection
rule with high probability ( Geifman and El-Yaniv, 2017 ) . SC-LEC calibrates
the threshold of a fixed predictor and uncertainty score, keeping this
statistical task separate from learning the answer or refusal policy.

blocks.en:
Probability calibration asks whether confidence values reflect observed
correctness frequencies. Temperature scaling is a standard post-hoc
approach to this problem ( Guo et al., 2017 ) . For language models, Kadavath et al. (2022) study self-evaluation of proposed answers and
prediction of whether a question can be answered. Tian et al. (2023) compare methods for eliciting confidence from models fine-tuned with human
feedback, while Xiong et al. (2024) evaluate prompting, sampling,
and aggregation for confidence calibration and failure prediction.
These studies concern the information in confidence scores and their
empirical calibration. The finite-sample risk of a threshold selected
using calibration data is a separate statistical question.
Other signals compare generated responses: SelfCheckGPT uses consistency
across samples to detect potentially nonfactual content without an external
database ( Manakul et al., 2023 ) , and semantic uncertainty groups
equivalent answers ( Kuhn et al., 2023 ; Farquhar et al., 2024 ) .
Such signals can inform the score supplied to a calibration procedure.
Their ability to rank errors does not by itself certify the selected
answers’ error rate.

blocks.en:
Conformal prediction controls prediction-set
coverage ( Angelopoulos and Bates, 2023 ) , but the set or error event being
controlled matters in language generation. Conformal Language Modeling
calibrates sampling and rejection to produce a set containing at least one
acceptable response, with high probability over calibration data of meeting
the specified test-coverage target ( Quach et al., 2024 ) . This controls
an event about the output set, rather than the error rate among individually
accepted answers. Mohri and Hashimoto (2024) instead calibrate a back-off
rule that reduces output specificity to obtain entailment-based factuality
guarantees. Their marginal guarantee is defined relative to a reference
and an entailment oracle, and changes the content of the output rather than
only selecting whether to return a fixed answer.
ConU and SConU also study conformal uncertainty and selection for language
models ( Wang et al., 2024 ; Wang et al., 2025b ) . For batch selection, Jin and Candès (2023) combine conformal p-values with multiple testing
to control false discovery rate under their stated assumptions.
This is an expectation of a random error fraction, as is the batch target
in Conformal Labeling ( Huang et al., 2026 ) . Marginal SCER is instead
the ratio of expected accepted errors to expected acceptance. Selective
conformal risk control studies selected prediction sets ( Xu et al., 2025 ) .
These distinctions concern estimands and decision rules, rather than a
general ordering of guarantee strength.

Risk-controlling prediction sets accommodate losses beyond set
miscoverage ( Bates et al., 2021 ) . LEC expresses marginal
selection-conditioned risk as a linear expectation
constraint ( Wang et al., 2026a ) . For adaptive non-monotonic calibration,
the full-data/leave-one-out analysis of Angelopoulos (2026) connects a reference rule to a calibration-fitted rule, building on the
broader relationship between stability and
generalization ( Bousquet and Elisseeff, 2002 ) . Our analysis accounts for the reserve and signed stability gap,
and specializes the crossing bounds to anchored threshold search.
The explicit bounds certify a nonpositive linear-risk endpoint without
estimating stability by a bootstrap plug-in.

Learn then Test (LTT) combines valid tests with multiplicity control
for high-probability risk guarantees, including non-monotonic
risks ( Angelopoulos et al., 2025 ) . Our LTT-CP instantiation tests
an independent selection-score grid with exact binomial tests and
Bonferroni correction. For a candidate j j , let N j N_{j} and K j K_{j} be its
accepted and erroneous-accepted counts on the testing sample. Its
one-sided test uses p j = Pr { Bin ( N j , α ) ≤ K j } . p_{j}=\Pr\{\operatorname{Bin}(N_{j},\alpha)\leq K_{j}\}. (52) Under i.i.d. sampling, conditional on N j N_{j} , the error count is
binomial with parameter equal to that fixed candidate’s selective risk.
The predictor, score, and all candidates must be independent of the
testing observations. We test all L = 20 L=20 candidates at δ / L \delta/L and
select the largest passing threshold; candidates with N j = 0 N_{j}=0 cannot
pass, and no passing candidate yields abstention. This is equivalent to
requiring a one-sided Clopper–Pearson upper bound at level 1 − δ / L 1-\delta/L to be at most α \alpha . Bonferroni allows dependence
between the candidate tests and protects the subsequent selection.
Thus LTT certifies the realized fitted policy, whereas SC-LEC’s upstream
event certifies calibration-averaged marginal risk for a scan over
final-calibration order statistics. LTT may be preferable for a fixed
deployment, and valid testing constructions can also accommodate
adaptive candidates. The present experiments do not establish
an operational advantage over LTT at a common guarantee.
